title: Glioblastoma with a primitive neuronal component: A case report
case_prompt: A 57-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of sudden-onset headache accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She denied loss of consciousness, focal weakness, speech disturbance, seizures, or memory changes. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus and remote obstetric hemorrhage requiring transfusion. On admission, vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 277.6 U/L. Brain MRI demonstrated a 6.3 × 5.5 cm irregular, well‐demarcated lesion at the junction of the left parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with ring-like enhancement after contrast and surrounding edema. After glycemic control with insulin, she underwent neurosurgical resection. Intraoperatively, the mass in the mesial temporal lobe was solid, whereas the adjacent paraventricular component was cystic and contained yellow purulent fluid. Both lesions were separately excised and sent for histopathologic examination. Postoperatively, she remained hemodynamically stable with intact cognition and motor strength, but with persistent speech clarity difficulties.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Brain abscess — considered because of cystic lesion with purulent fluid; excluded once pathology demonstrated tumor rather than infection: “the cystic portion of the mass contained yellow purulent fluid, which...could be mistaken for a brain abscess.”  
2. Papillary glioneuronal tumor — considered due to biphasic glial and neuronal components; excluded because these tumors are low-grade and display “very rare necrosis and mitotic figures.”  
3. Glioneuronal tumor with neuropil-like islands — considered for its mixed astrocytic and neural islands; excluded because such tumors are “characterized by a background of infiltrating astrocytomas with islands of neuropil-like tissue surrounded by oligodendrocyte-like or atypical neuron-like cells,” unlike the high-grade features here.  
4. Small cell glioblastoma — considered as a high-grade glial neoplasm with small cells; excluded because the lesion’s primitive neuronal component showed strong neuronal marker expression: “Strong expression of Syn, p53, NSE, Ki-67 (90%) and TTF-1 was observed in the PNC.”
